I have already noted in the introduction to the Choeph. p. 12 that the last argument of Apollo seems directed against the old view, according to which the bond of the child with the mother, which was not in doubt, was considered the most sacred, while with the higher culture that followed from the introduction of marriage, the father received at least equal standing. Cf. Telemachus' jest ⟦1⟧ 215: ⟦2⟧· ⟦3⟧· ⟦4⟧, and Clearchus in Athenaeus XIII 555 D (cited by Wecklein): ⟦5⟧, ⟦6⟧. ⟦7⟧, ⟦8⟧. Cf. above on 640 ff. The theory that the father is the true begetter is also clearly found in Euripides, who will have taken it from here and uses it in the Or. (552 ff.) for the same purpose, see also (Schütz) Frg. 1048. Anaxagoras (see Wilamowitz Übers. p. 43, 1) seems to have taught the same, Aristot. De gen. anim. Δ 1 p. 763 e 31 ff. (Diels Vorsokrat. 325); but another testimony contradicts this (ibid. no. 111). Paley also cites ⟦9⟧: ⟦10⟧ (lacunose), ⟦11⟧.
